subject: Consideration of batch and gender effects

messages.author: d3cb5abb144524de
messages.subject: Consideration of batch and gender effects
parts:
Dear MSstats team,

Currently I am doing the analysis of a control-disease comparison. Due to sample management I had to split the sample preparation (n = 76) in two batches; each including 4 QC samples. I accounted for disease and gender for the blocking and randomization of the samples into the two batches.

I acquired data for non-enriched and peptide level enriched samples for PTMs of interest and analyzed the data in Skyline. I have formatted the data for MSstats PTM and can run the analysis to completion by doing a single control-disease comparion.

However, there is one thing I am not sure yet (and please excuse my ignorance in this matter): do I have to do something else with MSstats to account for batch effects or gender-specific effects? Or was this accounted by the randomization to avoid bias in the sample grouping?

Thank you for your time and help!
Sincerely,
Juan C.

PS: attached is a slide with the experimental design

messages.author: 2889aa2e61425c8e
messages.subject: Re: Consideration of batch and gender effects
parts:
Hi Juan,

This is a nice design! Since your sample allocation balances disease and gender in every batch, you avoided confounding between these factors and the batch. The ‘global’ normalization with MSstats will account for systematic changes between the batches that affect all the proteins. The analysis with MSstats without any extra adjustments will not be subject to the confounding bias.  

You can choose to extend the analysis by accounting for the batch and gender effects at the level of individual proteins. This will reduce the estimated standard errors and increase the sensitivity. However, since the number of replicates in each combination of batch/condition/gender is relatively small, this will introduce the risk of overfitting (and false positives).

If you decide to do the adjustments, you implement this by creating a new ‘condition’, which is a combination of all the levels of disease.gender.batch (i.e., 8 total). Then create a contrast where you compare two diseases on average over all genders and batches. This will effectively perform the adjustment.

Btw, regardless of what you do, do not include in the MSstats analysis the ’total pool’ samples. Since they represent multiple individuals (as opposed to one individual at a time), they do not have the same structure of variation as the rest of the samples, and will not be well represented by the model.

HTH
Olga

Thank you for your comments and the very helpful clarification!

I will have a look at the suggested adjustments, but, as you pointed out the concerns for false positive results, I am inclined to keep the initial setup.

I used the "total pool samples" for several sample preparation and system performance QCs (some summary plots below), but I am filtering out these results before going into the MSstats pipeline.
